---
order: 3
unit: why
title: Why do you do it?
summary: "People do schoolwork for lots of reasons at once: some push you from outside, some are your own. Goals differ too: getting better, looking good, or not looking bad. Marks are the scoreboard: worth knowing, but not the same as getting better, and aiming only at the scoreboard can steer you toward easy tasks and shortcuts. Your learning coach asks why this matters to you, and sets goals about what you'll do."
language: science
shape: primer
hook: "Ava did her maths homework last night. Why? Probably more than one reason."
---
Everyone in this workshop is made up. You'll think about your own reasons at the end, privately.

## Think first

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Starting with a made-up learner's reasons, not the student's own. Most students expect one reason; the reveal is a mix."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "Ava did her maths homework last night. What was her reason most likely to be?"
  options: ["She had to: it was due", "She wanted a good mark", "She wants to get better at fractions", "Several of these at once"]
  actual: "Here's what Ava said: \"It's due tomorrow, and I don't want to get in trouble. I want to do well on the test. And honestly, fractions keep tripping me up, so I want to get them.\" That's three reasons at once, which is normal. Most people have a mix."
```

## The idea

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Two ideas that go together but aren't the same: why you do it (reasons) and what you're aiming for (goals). Then the planted slip: a good mark means you've learned it."
tasks:
  - insight: "Reasons range from pushed (outside you) to owned (yours). A reason that started outside you can still be one you own."
    check:
      type: sort
      q: "Sort these made-up learners' reasons for doing their homework. Is each one mostly pushing them from outside, or one they own?"
      options: ["Pushed: from outside", "Owned: it matters to them"]
      items:
        - ["\"I'll get a detention if I don't.\"", "Pushed: from outside"]
        - ["\"My parents will check.\"", "Pushed: from outside"]
        - ["\"I'd feel bad if everyone else did it and I didn't.\"", "Pushed: from outside", "This one comes from inside your head, but it's still a push: guilt or worry, not wanting it."]
        - ["\"I want to understand how volcanoes work. It's interesting.\"", "Owned: it matters to them"]
        - ["\"I need fractions for science next year, and I want to be ready.\"", "Owned: it matters to them", "It's for something else, but it's a reason this learner agrees with and owns."]
        - ["\"I want to get better at writing, so I can write my own stories.\"", "Owned: it matters to them"]
  - insight: "The goals grid: what you're aiming for. Emphasis on getting better, looking good and not looking bad."
    check:
      type: sort
      q: "Now sort what each learner is aiming for."
      options: ["Getting better", "Not slipping back", "Looking good", "Not looking bad"]
      items:
        - ["\"I want to be able to do the hard questions by the end of term.\"", "Getting better"]
        - ["\"I want to beat my score from last time.\"", "Getting better", "Comparing with your own past self is about getting better."]
        - ["\"I want the top mark in the class.\"", "Looking good"]
        - ["\"I want people to see I'm good at this.\"", "Looking good"]
        - ["\"I just don't want to be the worst.\"", "Not looking bad"]
        - ["\"I won't put my hand up in case I'm wrong.\"", "Not looking bad"]
        - ["\"I don't want to forget what I learned last term.\"", "Not slipping back"]
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: "working.txt#nib"
      text: "Nib has a fractions quiz next week. Click the line where Nib's thinking first goes wrong."
      answer: 2
      fault: logic
      misconception: good-mark-means-learned
      explain: "Line 2: practising only the easy questions gets Nib a good practice score but doesn't make Nib any better at the hard ones. Nib was steering toward the scoreboard, not toward getting better."
```

**Why you do it.** Some reasons **push** you from outside: a deadline, a detention, someone checking. Some you **own**: it's interesting, or it matters for something you care about. Most people have a mix, and pushed reasons aren't bad: deadlines get things done. But reasons you own usually help you keep going when it gets hard.

**What you're aiming for.** Goals fit into a grid:

| | Aiming **for** something | Aiming to **avoid** something |
|---|---|---|
| **Compared with yourself or the task** | Getting better | Not slipping back |
| **Compared with other people** | Looking good | Not looking bad |

You can have more than one at once, and getting better and doing well often go together fine. The one to watch is **not looking bad**: it can make you avoid hard questions, skip putting your hand up, or give up so it doesn't look like you tried. The coach notices worry like that and points back at getting better.

**Marks are the scoreboard.** They're worth knowing: they tell you something about how it went. But the scoreboard isn't the same as getting better. If you steer only toward the scoreboard, you might pick easy tasks, take shortcuts, reread instead of testing yourself, or fall apart after a bad mark. There's a difference between doing the moves **for the teacher** and doing them **for yourself**.

**Two moves your coach can use:**

- **Beat your own best.** Compare with your past self, not with other people: "more right than last week".
- **What you'll do, not just what you'll get.** "Get an A" is what you'll get. "Test myself on five questions each night" is what you'll do, and you're in charge of that.

And one question: **"Why does this matter to me right now?"** Sometimes the honest answer is "it's due". That's fine. See if you can find one reason of your own as well.

## Check

```step
stage: practise
tasks:
  - check:
      type: sort
      q: "Is each goal about what you'll do, or what you'll get?"
      options: ["What you'll do", "What you'll get"]
      items:
        - ["Get an A on the test", "What you'll get"]
        - ["Test myself on five questions each night", "What you'll do"]
        - ["Come in the top three", "What you'll get"]
        - ["Read my draft aloud and fix one sentence", "What you'll do"]
        - ["Ask about the bit I don't get on Tuesday", "What you'll do"]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Raj gets a C on a science test after working hard. Which thought sounds most like his learning coach?"
      options: ["\"Which questions did I lose marks on, and what can I practise?\"", "\"Everyone did better than me, so I should give up on science.\"", "\"Next time I'll only do the questions I know I'll get right.\"", "\"Marks don't matter, so I won't look at the test.\""]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "That's a not-looking-bad thought. It stops the learning.", "That's steering to the scoreboard: a better mark, but no better at science.", "The mark is worth knowing. It shows Raj where to work next."]
      explain: "The coach reads the scoreboard for information, then points at getting better."
```

## Apply

```step
stage: make
insight: "Students place their own reasons and goals privately. Share only what you're comfortable with."
check:
  type: reflect
  text: "I've thought about my own reasons and goals for one subject."
```

Pick one subject. Just for yourself:

- What are your reasons for doing the work? Which ones push you, and which do you own?
- Which box of the grid are you mostly aiming for? Is that helping you?

You don't need to write this down or share it. If something surprised you, you can tell your partner, but you don't have to.

## Try

```step
stage: run
insight: "Turning a what-you'll-get goal into a what-you'll-do goal for a real task this week."
check:
  type: reasoning
  q: "Pick a real task from another subject this week. Write one goal about what you'll do (not what you'll get), and one reason it matters to you."
  placeholder: "This week in … I will … It matters to me because …"
  models:
    - title: "Maths"
      text: "This week in maths I'll do three practice questions each night without looking at the examples first. It matters because I keep forgetting the method in tests."
    - title: "English"
      text: "For my persuasive piece, I'll read my draft aloud on Wednesday and fix the two weakest sentences. It matters because I want people to actually agree with me."
  criteria:
    - "My goal is something I'll do, and I'm in charge of whether it happens."
    - "I gave a reason that's mine, even if there's also a deadline."
```

This stays in your browser. Nobody sees it unless you show them.

```teacher
summary: Students guess why a made-up learner did her homework (a mix), sort
  reasons into pushed and owned, sort goals into the four boxes of the goals
  grid, find Nib's slip (practising only easy questions to get a good score),
  and meet marks as the scoreboard. They sort goals into what you'll do and what
  you'll get, pick the coach's response to a disappointing mark, privately place
  their own reasons and goals, and write a what-you'll-do goal for a real task
  this week.
time: 40
timing: Think first 4 min · The idea 16 min · Check 7 min · Apply 4 min · Try 6
  min (plus the class discussion)
goals:
  - I can tell reasons that push me from outside apart from reasons I own.
  - I can explain the difference between getting better and looking good, and
    why marks aren't the same as getting better.
  - I can set a goal about what I'll do, not just what I'll get.
struggle: "Students may hear 'reasons you own are better' as 'wanting a good
  mark is bad'. Keep saying: a mix is normal, pushed reasons get things done,
  and marks are worth knowing. The thing to watch is steering only toward the
  scoreboard, or only away from looking bad."
before: >
  **Grades, named openly.** This workshop says plainly that marks pull on how
  students study. Students in a grade-driven system are self-regulating, often
  toward the grade; the coach still asks what they're steering toward. Barr's
  distinctions give the language: surface compliance (doing the moves for the
  teacher) versus genuine self-regulated learning (using them for yourself), and
  mastery versus performance goals. Torrance's "criteria compliance" (steering
  to the rubric rather than the learning) describes the same pull from the
  assessment side.


  **Reasons.** Pushed versus owned is a plain version of the motivation
  continuum in self-determination theory (Ryan and Deci): reasons range from
  external (detention, rewards), through guilt and worry (pushed, though inside
  your head), to "identified" reasons (external in origin but owned, like
  needing fractions for next year) and interest. Most students hold a mix
  (Vansteenkiste and colleagues 2009, motivational profiles). Barr cautions
  against "intrinsic good, extrinsic bad", and so does this lesson.


  **Goals grid.** Elliot and McGregor's (2001) 2×2 of achievement goals:
  mastery-approach (getting better), mastery-avoidance (not slipping back),
  performance-approach (looking good) and performance-avoidance (not looking
  bad). Shown in full, with emphasis on three boxes; mastery-avoidance is shown
  lightly. Goals are what you aim for, and reasons are why: they're linked, not
  the same. Several goals at once is normal, and getting better and doing well
  often sit together (Barron and Harackiewicz, multiple goals).
  Performance-avoidance is the one most linked to avoiding challenge and giving
  up; performance-approach has mixed findings.


  **Two moves.** Growth goals, or beating your own best (Martin; NSW growth goal
  setting), and process goals before outcome goals (Zimmerman and Kitsantas
  1999), both from Barr's goal-setting work. "Is this worth it to me?" is task
  value (Barr; Eccles's expectancy, value and cost: can I do it, is it worth it,
  what does it cost me).


  **Feelings.** Worry about looking bad is part of this lesson; the coach
  notices it and points back at getting better.


  **Personal reflection.** The discussion uses only made-up learners. Apply is
  private, and the Try box stays in the student's browser. Students share only
  what they're comfortable with; nothing is collected or marked. If a student
  says something that suggests real distress about marks or pressure at home,
  follow your school's wellbeing process.
running:
  - "Think first: take a show of hands for each option, then read Ava's three
    reasons aloud."
  - "The idea: put the goals grid on the board. Place one made-up learner's
    thought in each box as a class before students sort the rest."
  - "The idea: say plainly that marks matter and are worth knowing. The point is
    what you steer toward."
  - "Check: for Raj, ask what each of the other three thoughts would lead him to
    do next week."
  - Apply is private. Don't ask which box students are in.
  - "Try: offer the two models to anyone stuck. Nothing is handed in."
stuck:
  - see: A student says they only do homework because they have to.
    ask: That's honest, and a lot of people would say the same. Is there any part of
      it that's useful to you, even a small bit?
    fix: Pushed reasons are normal. See if there's one reason of your own as well;
      if not, that's fine for now.
  - see: A student thinks wanting a good mark is bad.
    ask: Can you want a good mark and want to get better at the same time?
    fix: Yes. Marks are worth knowing. The trouble is steering only toward the mark.
  - see: A student can't turn 'get an A' into something they'll do.
    ask: What would someone who gets an A in that subject actually do each week?
    fix: Pick one of those things and make it the goal.
stretch: Think of something you do outside school because you want to. What
  makes that reason your own, and could any of it carry over to a school
  subject?
support: "The goals grid on a card with one example in each box, and two goal
  starters: 'This week I will…' and 'Better than last time at…'."
leads: >
  Next: when easy fools you. Why some study feels like learning but isn't much.


  Teachers: For Learning skills teachers has notes on assessing self-regulated
  learning (keep it formative).
exit:
  q: Turn 'get a better mark in science' into a goal about what you'll do.
  a: Any specific action the student controls, such as 'test myself on the key
    words twice this week' or 'redo the questions I got wrong'.
explain: >
  People do schoolwork for a **mix of reasons**: some **push** you from outside,
  some you **own**. Both are normal.


  Goals differ too: **getting better**, **not slipping back**, **looking good**
  or **not looking bad**. Watch out for "not looking bad": it can make you avoid
  hard things.


  **Marks are the scoreboard**: worth knowing, but not the same as getting
  better. Your learning coach asks "why does this matter to me?", tries to beat
  your own best, and sets goals about **what you'll do**, not just what you'll
  get.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: If there were no marks at all, would people learn more or less at school?
    prompts:
      - What do marks tell you that's useful?
      - What do marks make people do that doesn't help them learn?
      - Would you still do the work?
    notes: "An open debate with good arguments both ways. Bring it back to the
      scoreboard: worth knowing, not the same as getting better. Keep it about
      people in general."
  activities:
    - at: investigate
      kind: activity
      title: The grid
      minutes: 5
      do: >
        Draw the goals grid. Where would each of these go? "Beat my last score."
        "Top of the class." "Just don't be the worst."
      notes: On the board, as a class, with made-up thoughts only. Point out that one
        learner can have thoughts in several boxes.
    - at: end
      kind: discussion
      title: For the teacher or for yourself?
      minutes: 6
      do: >
        In pairs: Mia writes a plan for her essay because the teacher checks it.
        Kai writes one because it helps him. The plans look the same. Does it
        matter which reason they had?
      notes: "Aim for: the plan is the same, but Kai will probably keep doing it when
        nobody checks. That's the difference between doing it for the teacher
        and for yourself."
  questions:
    - at: investigate
      title: Which box?
      type: question
      q: Sam doesn't put his hand up in case he's wrong. Which goal is that?
      options:
        - Not looking bad
        - Getting better
        - Looking good
      answer: 0
      explain: Avoiding looking bad can mean missing the chance to find out and get
        better.
```
